ANALYSIS_EMBEDDINGS: **Assessment.** The skip-gram embeddings clearly capture meaningful *topical and functional* relations: the neighbours of عدالت (court) are جج (judge), درخواست (petition), مقدمے (case), استدعا (plea), سزا (sentence), اپیل (appeal), کورٹ, وکیل (lawyer) and دائر (filed); فوج (army) sits next to کمانڈر, عسکری, کمان and افواج; معیشت (economy) next to معاشی, قلت (shortage), زر (as in افراطِ زر, inflation), قیمت (price) and مہنگائی (all shown in A1-stemmed form in the table). Five of the ten analogy tests are solved within the top-3 (four of them at rank 1): country→leader, country→demonym, first name→surname and commodity→unit — relations that are repeated many times in this news corpus — whereas relations attested only a handful of times (capitals, male/female kinship, institution→professional, armed group→territory) fail. With only 434k tokens the vectors also absorb corpus-specific collocations: پاکستان is closest to cricket words (کرکٹ، لیگ، بورڈ، ہاکی) because "Pakistan cricket board / league / women's team" are frequent phrases, and the A1 stemmer conflates آبادی (population) with the *-abad* of city names, so the neighbours of *Aabadi* are places (اسلام آباد، لاہور، کابل، راولپنڈی).
ANALYSIS_CONDITIONS: **Discussion.** On the 20 labelled pairs the PPMI baseline (C1) has the highest MRR (0.342; 4 related words ranked first, median rank 5), followed by skip-gram on the cleaned corpus (C3, 0.290), while skip-gram on raw text (C2, 0.236) and the 200-dimensional model (C4, 0.235) are lowest. With only 0.43 M tokens, explicit count statistics are a strong baseline: frequent, tightly co-occurring pairs (government–minister, army–general, Russia–Ukraine, Imran–Khan) are ranked first by PPMI directly, whereas skip-gram must learn them through stochastic optimisation from the same few contexts. Preprocessing clearly helps the neural model: C3 beats C2, and C2's neighbour lists are split over inflected, izafat-marked or punctuation-attached variants (نظامِ، تحریکِ، اسرائیلی، دیشی، فوجی) — the raw text has 19,423 types against 10,943 after cleaning, so each surface form gets fewer training contexts and the 10k vocabulary covers less of the text. Doubling the dimension does not help: C4 reaches a lower training loss than C3 (2.684 vs 2.769) but a lower MRR, i.e. the extra capacity is spent fitting this small corpus rather than producing better similarities. Among the neural models the best embeddings are therefore C3 (d = 100 on the cleaned corpus), and PPMI is best overall on this small test set; note that with 20 pairs a single rank change moves the MRR by up to 0.05, so the C1–C3 gap is indicative rather than conclusive.
ANALYSIS_POS_CONFUSIONS: **Why these tags are confused.** (1) **NOUN ↔ UNK** (58 errors; 44 of the 99 gold-UNK tokens are predicted NOUN, 14 gold nouns are predicted UNK). In the silver annotation, UNK is what the rule-based tagger assigns to words that are in neither the lexicon nor covered by a morphology or context rule — rare nouns, names, transliterated English words — while the same kind of word becomes NOUN as soon as it stands before a case marker. The label therefore depends on rules the BiLSTM only sees indirectly: it calls most gold-UNK words NOUN (often linguistically right) and occasionally predicts UNK for real nouns such as انجام (completion) or صحافی (journalist); UNK is the weakest class (F1 0.45). (2) **NOUN ↔ ADJ** (43; 31 of them gold nouns predicted ADJ). The A1 stemmer strips the nisba suffix *-ی* that separates many adjectives from their nouns (سیاسی → سیاس, بہتری → بہتر), so the cleaned token alone is ambiguous, and names or nouns in adjectival positions (جون, پیشکش, سیاست in سیاست دان) are pulled towards ADJ; some gold labels are themselves wrong: بہتر in "نظام میں بہتری کے لیے" is the noun *improvement*, but the tagger's stem fallback labelled it ADJ, so here the model's NOUN is the correct tag. (3) **NOUN ↔ VERB** (18). Urdu conjunct verbs (noun + کرنا/ہونا) put nouns directly before verbal material, and stemming makes some nouns look like verb roots (سامنا *facing* → سام before ہے; اصلاح *reform*).
ANALYSIS_ABLATIONS: **Findings.** **A1 (unidirectional)** is the most damaging change: −5.4 macro-F1 for POS and −23.5 F1 for NER. Urdu is head-final, so the disambiguating evidence usually comes *after* a token — whether کی is the genitive or the verb *did* is decided by a following auxiliary, and یہ/اس are determiners only if a noun follows — and for NER a forward-only model has to decide B-PER/B-LOC at the first token of an entity without seeing the surname, postposition or "… کے شہر" context that follows (its validation F1 also varies wildly across seeds, ±15.5). **A2 (no dropout)** has no measurable effect (POS −0.3, NER +1.1, both well within one standard deviation): with only 350 sentences, early stopping on validation F1 already limits over-fitting, so dropout between the two LSTM layers neither helps nor hurts here. **A3 (random initialisation)** costs 4.2 POS and 11.4 NER points: the C3 vectors bring distributional knowledge from the whole 434k-token corpus (which words behave like names, places, function words or verbs) that 350 labelled sentences cannot provide on their own. **A4 (softmax instead of CRF)** lowers mean NER F1 by 7.5 (62.4 ± 3.4 vs 69.9 ± 3.8), through both precision (66.5 vs 74.2) and recall (58.8 vs 66.1): per-token argmax decides every tag independently and ignores which tag sequences are valid (e.g. I-PER after O), whereas the CRF learns transition scores and decodes the best whole sequence with Viterbi. On seed 42 alone the softmax model happens to score higher (66.7 vs 64.8) — single runs on 55 test entities are noisy, which is why every comparison is reported over three seeds.
ANALYSIS_NER_ERRORS:
**Error analysis (fine-tuned BiLSTM-CRF, seed 42).** A span with the right tokens but the wrong type or boundaries counts as both a false positive and a false negative in conlleval.

*False positives*
1. **مصطف → ORG** (gold: مصطفیٰ نواز, PER). مصطف (the A1 stem of مصطفیٰ) never occurs in the 350 training sentences, so the model splits the unseen name into an ORG piece and a PER piece.
2. **نواز → PER** — the second half of the same name (نواز is I-PER twice in training); the span is too short.
3. **فاطمہ ثنا → PER** (gold: فاطمہ only). Here the *model is right*: Fatima Sana is Pakistan's women's cricket captain; the silver label is incomplete because ثنا (also 'praise') was deliberately left out of the given-name list.
4. **سعود → MISC** (gold O). This is the cricketer Saud Shakeel, but the A1 stemmer maps سعودی (Saudi) and the name سعود to the same token, which is MISC (5×) or part of LOC سعودی عرب (5×) in training, so the model reads 'Saudi'. The gold label is wrong too (should be PER): he is not in the gazetteer.
5. **پاکستان → LOC** inside پاکستان کرکٹ بورڈ (gold ORG). پاکستان is LOC in 31 of its 33 training occurrences and the three-token organisation name was seen once, so the model tags the country and misses the organisation.

*False negatives*
1. **مصطفیٰ نواز (PER)** — wrong boundaries/types, see FP 1–2.
2. **خیبر پختونخوا (LOC)** and 3. **پشاور (LOC)** in "فرزانہ علی خیبر پختونخوا کے شہر پشاور میں ..." — none of these tokens occurs in the training split, and the reporter-byline context (name + place + 'Aaj News') is unlike the training sentences.
4. **انور ابراہیم (PER)** — Malaysia's prime minister; both tokens are unseen in training and only 61 person entities are available to learn person contexts from.
5. **جیو نیوز (ORG)** — Geo News: unseen tokens inside quotation marks, and ORG is the rarest type (29 training entities; test F1 18.2).

**Overall:** the errors come mostly from (a) entities whose tokens never occur in the 350 training sentences, where the model must rely on context it has seen too few examples of, (b) the A1 stemmer merging different words (سعود), and (c) noise in the silver annotation itself (incomplete names, people missing from the gazetteer) — part of the measured error is annotation error, not model error.
ANALYSIS_COMPARISON:
**BiLSTM vs Transformer (answers to the five questions).**
1. **Accuracy.** The Transformer is more accurate on the test set: 78.4% vs 67.6% for seed 42 (+10.8 points) and 77.5 ± 3.4% vs 71.2 ± 3.4% over three seeds (+6.3), with macro-F1 64.7 vs 54.2; the seed-42 BiLSTM never predicts Politics and gets only one of the four Economy articles right.
2. **Convergence.** The BiLSTM converged in fewer epochs: its best validation epoch was 13/19/15 (mean 15.7) against 18/17/17 (mean 17.3) for the Transformer, and for seed 42 it left the majority-class baseline (47.4%) at epoch 6, whereas the Transformer stayed there for 7 epochs during warm-up and early training and reached its validation plateau (68.4%) at epoch 11 — although the BiLSTM's validation curve is much less stable (validation loss jumps from 0.63 to 1.22 between epochs 17 and 19).
3. **Speed.** The BiLSTM is about 2.2× faster per epoch (1.66 s vs 3.70 s): self-attention computes 257 × 257 scores per head in 4 heads × 4 layers plus a 512-wide feed-forward network at every position, and our from-scratch layer runs the four separately projected heads one after another, while the 2-layer LSTM is a single optimised library kernel whose cost grows only linearly with length and has fewer parameters (1.66 M vs 2.08 M).
4. **Attention.** The final-layer [CLS] attention concentrates on topic words: in the Sports article the three occurrences of کرکٹ (cricket) receive ≈ 0.05 attention each, about 7× more than any other token, followed by کھیل (sport) and پاکستان; in the Politics article the distribution is much flatter (maximum ≈ 0.008, about twice the uniform 1/256) and its top 12 mixes four occurrences of ٹرمپ (Trump) with کیوں (why), نہیں (not) and توڑ (break); in the Economy article رسد (supply) ranks first and وسط (from مشرقِ وسطیٰ, Middle East) appears twice. Frequent function words (کی، پر، نے) also collect attention as default positions, and the token-to-token maps show heads with different degrees of focus.
5. **Which architecture for 200–300 articles?** For this task, the Transformer: topic labels depend mainly on which topical keywords occur anywhere in the 256-token window, and [CLS] attention pools exactly that (in effect a learned, weighted bag of words), whereas the BiLSTM must carry the evidence through 256 sequential steps. The data is, however, too small for either model to be reliable — the Transformer needs warm-up and 8 epochs to leave the majority class and its macro-F1 varies by ±7 points across seeds, and its 6-point advantage corresponds to only 2–3 of the 37 test articles (on the 38 validation articles the seed-42 BiLSTM even scored higher, 76.3% vs 68.4%) — so the BiLSTM with pretrained embeddings remains the cheaper, faster-converging alternative.
